Hero.BasedInAyitiQuote: Programs should feel close to the streets they serve — not distant in a dashboard.

Story.Title: A grant workflow that grew into something public.
Story.Subtitle: IFundAyiti started inside Hubology as a way to review local ideas with care. It became its own site so applicants, donors, and communities could share one clear record.
Story.Paragraph1: That evolution was intentional. Private spreadsheets and closed inboxes make hope feel fragile. A public platform lets families track an application, lets donors see how gifts are used, and lets winners be celebrated without exposing every personal detail online.
Story.Paragraph2: We are still early — much of this site runs on demo content while official program details are finalized. The commitment is already real: run grants with transparency, respect, and a Haiti-first point of view.
Story.Callout: Small teams. Clear rules. Real names behind the work.

Principles.Title: Four principles that do not bend.
Principles.Subtitle: Not slogans for a homepage — standards we use when reviewing files, speaking with donors, and choosing winners.
Principles.Principle1Body: Application status, finalists, and winners are visible on a public site — not hidden behind private threads or opaque approvals.
Principles.Principle2Body: A vetting board reads each submission with neighborhood context in mind. Capital follows judgment, not algorithms alone.
Principles.Principle3Body: We ask for verification without spectacle. Proof protects the community; it should never feel like a performance of hardship.
Principles.Principle4Body: Donations pool into a single Program Fund. Grants go to selected winners — not to individual crowdfunding profiles.

Audiences.Title: Three groups, one shared outcome.
Audiences.Subtitle: IFundAyiti only works when builders, supporters, and neighbors all recognize themselves in the process.
Audiences.Audience1Body: Street cooks, plot tenders, repair crews, and corner inventors who need a first push — not another loan with impossible terms.
Audiences.Audience2Body: Give to a program you can explain to a friend: where money pools, how winners are chosen, and why names stay protected.
Audiences.Audience3Emotion: Impact should be visible on the block.
Audiences.Audience3Body: Better light, cleaner water, fuller stalls, safer lanes — the kind of change you notice on a walk home, not in a press release.

Governance.Title: Governance without mystery.
Governance.Subtitle: The home page walks through the grant lifecycle. Here is the accountability layer underneath it.
Governance.Step1Body: During an open cycle, builders submit ideas, IDs, and supporting documents through a structured public form.
Governance.Step2Body: The vetting board checks completeness, feasibility, and community fit. Approved applicants may appear as public finalists.
Governance.Step3Body: One winner is selected per period. Funds are transferred manually to verified recipients — outside individual campaign pages.

Connect.Title: Ready to go deeper?
Connect.Body: Grant rules and timelines live on the grants page. Questions about the program — or how to partner with us — belong in a conversation, not a repeated homepage pitch.

Cycle.OpenLead: The window is open — submit while dates allow.
Cycle.ClosedLead: Applications are closed for this period. Track status or prepare for the next cycle.
Cycle.MaxGrantNote: Requests above the maximum cannot be reviewed. Plan for materials, tools, stock, or launch costs you can show on paper.

Prepare.Title: Prepare your file with care.
Prepare.Subtitle: Incomplete applications slow everyone down. Gather these pieces first so your story reads clearly on the first pass.
Prepare.EligIntro: We look for builders rooted in Haiti with a project neighbors can recognize — not slide decks aimed at distant investors.
Prepare.EligItem1Body: You live and work locally, and you can carry out the proposed project where the community will feel it.
Prepare.EligItem2Body: Livelihoods, food, energy, water, education, craft, or similar needs — projects that improve daily life on the ground.
Prepare.EligItem3Body: Valid government ID and proof of address. Verification protects applicants, donors, and the vetting board alike.
Prepare.EligItem4Body: Your ask stays at or below $1,000 USD. Show exactly how each dollar moves the project forward.
Prepare.DocIntro: Required items are non-negotiable. Optional materials help reviewers picture your plan faster.
Prepare.DocItem1Body: Required — confirms you are the applicant behind the file.
Prepare.DocItem2Body: Required — ties the project to a real place reviewers can understand.
Prepare.DocItem3Body: Required — what you will do, what you need, and how funds will be spent.
Prepare.DocItem4Body: Required — who benefits, how soon, and why it matters on your block.
Prepare.DocItem5Body: Optional but strongly recommended — sketches, stall photos, or a simple plan go a long way.

Selection.Title: How selection actually works.
Selection.Subtitle: No hidden stages. Your status moves in public view — from first submission to one funded winner per cycle.
Selection.Step1Body: You receive confirmation and can track status with the email and date of birth used on the form.
Selection.Step2Body: The team checks completeness, feasibility, and community impact. Missing pieces may delay a decision.
Selection.Step3Emotion: Every applicant deserves a clear answer.
Selection.Step3Body: Strong approved applications may appear as public finalists for the current cycle.
Selection.Step4Body: Up to five finalists are highlighted publicly. One winner is chosen per period.
Selection.Step5Body: The selected winner receives up to $1,000. Funds are transferred manually to verified recipients — not through individual campaign pages.

FAQ.Title: Grant questions, answered plainly.
FAQ.Subtitle: Still unsure? Read the cycle above or contact the team before the window closes.
FAQ.A1: Applicants should be based in Haiti and able to carry out a community-focused project. Final eligibility is confirmed during review.
FAQ.A2: The maximum requested grant amount is $1,000. Requests above that amount cannot be considered.
FAQ.A3: A government-issued ID, proof of address, and a project description are required. A business plan or supporting images are recommended.
FAQ.A4: Applications are accepted only during an open grant cycle. Dates are published on the Grants page.
FAQ.A5: The IFundAyiti team reviews completeness, feasibility, and expected community impact. Status then moves from submitted to under review.
FAQ.A6: Approved applicants with the strongest community case may become finalists for the current cycle.
FAQ.A7: One finalist is selected as the winner per application period according to IFundAyiti’s selection process.
